transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (Cascade Head of ML), Priya Shah (Cascade Platform), James Lee (Cascade CTO)

Summary: Redwood Optimize deep-dive on batching and KV/prefix cache strategies to reduce token cost while meeting p95 latency goal. Demo of the cost model spreadsheet and recommended config.

[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate you squeezing this in, um we'll kick off, i'm ethan from redwood inference, with sofia on the se side
[00:07] Alex (Cascade): hey ethan, thanks, excited to see the optimize walkthrough we read the doc but wanted the live numbers
[00:12] Sofia (Redwood): cool i'll share my screen, quick agenda: batching basics, prefix vs KV cache, cost model assumptions, recommendations specific to cascade's traffic, then next steps
[00:22] James (Cascade): sounds good. our main constraints: target p95 < 150ms for UX flows, and monthly infra spend needs to be under $45k for inference, otherwise ops will push back
[00:34] Ethan: got it, and what are your typical qps and avg tokens?
[00:39] Alex: currently peak qps is ~220 req/s, avg tokens per request is 80, with bursts to 400 occasionally during campaign spikes
[00:48] Sofia: ok that's helpful. so first, batching: the engine does continuous batching, we can tune max batch size and timeout window. pitch is you get throughput wins but it can add latency if you increase the wait window
[01:02] Alex: yes, we saw in our PoC with other vendors that batching reduced cost but sometimes doubled p95; we can't lose the UX
[01:10] Sofia: totally. recommended starting point is small micro-batches with short timeout: e.g., max batch 32, timeout 12ms for chat-like workloads. for embeddings or async jobs you can batch larger and tolerate 200-500ms windows
[01:24] [01:24] Priya (Cascade): sorry quick q - how does prefix caching differ from KV cache? we use the terms interchangeably sometimes
[01:29] Sofia: good question. prefix caching stores initial token prefixes/hidden states for repeated prompts, so it's very effective for templated flows. KV cache is the transformer KV cache persisted across steps to avoid re-computation during multi-turn sessions. both reduce token compute but different hit patterns
[01:47] Ethan: and in our runtime we support both; prefix cache is great for standardized onboarding flows and short fixed prompts, KV cache shines for long-running sessions with lots of revisits
[01:58] Alex: ok so for our payments flows which are multi-turn but short per turn, which do you recommend?
[02:04] Sofia: probably a hybrid. prefix cache for common system prompts (consent, onboarding) and KV cache when sessions exceed N turns - you can evict aggressively to control memory. our recommendation table maps hit rate to cost savings
[02:19] [02:19] Sofia: (shares spreadsheet) here's the cost model. assumptions: gpus priced at $X/hr for dedicated, quantized CPU options for lower throughput, token generation cost per sec, and we model hit rates of 0%, 20%, 50% for caches
[02:34] Alex: can you walk through the math for the 20% hit rate case?
[02:38] Sofia: sure - baseline w/o cache: 220 qps * 80 tokens * 30 days * 3600 = big token count, then convert to GPU hours based on tokens/sec throughput. with 20% KV hit we subtract recompute tokens for those hits, giving about 18% cost reduction for generation tokens, plus batching adds another 12% when tuned
[02:56] James: does the model include increased memory footprint cost for KV cache?
[03:01] Sofia: yes we add RAM overhead and slightly lower batching efficiency at high hit rates because cache hits short-circuit earlier, but net is still positive in most scenarios. we also show tradeoffs for keeping N sessions in memory vs rehydrating from prefix store on demand
[03:18] Alex: any surprises in the spreadsheet? like cases where caching makes things worse?
[03:22] Sofia: if your hit rate is very low (<5%) and you have very short sequences, the cache management overhead (eviction, memory pressure) can cost you. also if your workload is extremely bursty and you rely on tiny timeouts to keep latency low, batching wins are limited
[03:38] [03:38] Ethan: we also included fallback routing: if dedicated pool is saturated we'll route to hosted or quantized model variant. that preserves availability but changes unit cost; we show that in the cost-by-scenario tab
[03:51] Priya: security: do you do KMS for encryption at rest for cache data? we need to ensure that session data isn't logged in plain text
[03:58] Ethan: yes, private deployments allow customer-managed KMS/HSM keys and audit logs. for hosted we offer encryption at rest and RBAC; we can push SOC2 artifact pack - i'll include that in the follow-up
[04:10] Alex: nice. on the latency side, you said batching windows around 12ms, how consistent is that under 220 qps?
[04:16] Sofia: with continuous batching, at 220 qps and avg tokens 80, you'll see good packing into batches of 16-32 within the 12ms window on gpus; p95 stays sub 150ms, but we recommend running the 48-hour benchmark with your traffic to validate
[04:31] Alex: can you simulate our traffic? we can provide traces
[04:34] Sofia: yes - action: send CSV with timestamps and tokens, we will run the cost model and a simulated run in the staging dedicated pool
[04:41] James: what about model variants? can we fallback to a smaller quantized variant when queue grows?
[04:46] Ethan: yes, smart routing policies can route by latency or cost. you can set canary and automatic fallback to a cheaper quantized model if latency spikes, and we keep traces to compare quality regression
[04:55] Alex: what's the expected uplift from batching + 20% kv hit + smart routing?
[04:59] Sofia: combined we show ~28-35% unit cost reduction in the mid-case. worst-case about 10% if hit rates are low; best-case up to 50% with very predictable patterns and high hit rates
[05:12] Priya: any infra asks from our side for the pilot?
[05:15] Ethan: we'll need VPC peering details for private deployment or a staging API key for hosted; sample traffic CSV and a contact for network/security folks to sign the NDA if needed
[05:26] Alex: timeline: if we get the CSV today could you start the simulation next week?
[05:30] Sofia: yes we can run simulations starting 2026-05-04 and share results in 4-5 business days
[05:36] James: ok i'll loop in security, but high level this looks promising. can you also send a short doc that explains eviction policies for KV cache?
[05:45] Ethan: sure, i'll include an 'KV eviction patterns' note - typical policies: LRU with TTL, size-based eviction per customer, and session-tiering for VIP users
[05:55] Alex: one thing - in prior vendors we saw transcription glitches in logs, sometimes method names got munged, is that something you see?
[06:01] Sofia: sometimes the auto-transcripts scramble acronyms (KVS vs KV cache), but operational logs are structured and separate, we can show the log schema
[06:10] Ethan: recap & next steps: i'll send pricing + SOC2/security pack; sofia will run cost model with sample traffic; customer to provide CSV and compliance scope; schedule pilot kickoff week of 2026-05-04
[06:22] Alex: yep that works for us
[06:25] Priya: thanks all
[06:26] Ethan: thanks everyone, talk soon

End of transcript.
